title: Latex-ite Ultra Shield vs Airport Grade: Which Pail to Buy?
h1: Latex-ite Ultra Shield vs Airport Grade
query: latex-ite ultra shield vs airport grade
keywords: is ultra shield a good asphalt sealer
description: Ultra Shield has a 10-year warranty and a 40°F minimum on its 2019 sheet; Airport Grade needs 55°F. Both cover 300-500 sq ft a pail and cure in 24-48 hours.
dek: Same coverage, same cure time, same prep: the difference is the weather window, the film and the warranty.
quickAnswer: Buy Ultra Shield if you are sealing in cool weather (its 2019 data sheet allows 40°F and rising, against 55°F for Airport Grade), want Latex-ite's longest warranty (10 years on the sheet) or want the gel formula and UV-protection claim. Buy Airport Grade if it is warm, the driveway is sound and you reseal every few years anyway: it covers the same 300 to 500 square feet per pail and cures in the same 24 to 48 hours for less money.
intro: Latex-ite sells two driveway sealers that sit side by side on most shelves with similar pails and a clear price gap: Ultra Shield and Airport Grade (sold today as Airport Grade+). This page answers whether the dearer pail is better, what the 10-year and 4- or 5-year ratings really mean, and which one suits cold, hot or snowy climates.

Everything here comes from Latex-ite's published technical data sheets (Latex-ite is made by Dalton Enterprises of Cheshire, Connecticut), label directions and the general chemistry of asphalt-emulsion sealers. We have not applied these sealers ourselves. Data sheets get revised; where revisions disagree we say so, and the label on the pail you buy wins.

blocks.p: Read the table as two pails with one set of directions. Coverage, cure time, rain window, applicator and prep are identical, so switching from Airport Grade to Ultra Shield does not change how many pails you buy, how you apply them or how long the driveway is closed. The decision is about weather, film and price.

sections.h: Is Latex-ite Ultra Shield Better Than Airport Grade?

blocks.p: Yes on paper: Ultra Shield is Latex-ite's top-of-the-line sealer and Airport Grade is the mid-tier product. Both are water-based asphalt emulsions modified with polymers. What the extra money buys with Ultra Shield is a more flexible polymer system, a gel consistency that spreads more easily, a UV-protection claim, a cold-weather cure technology Latex-ite calls ThermaSEAL, and a longer warranty.

Whether that is worth paying for depends on two things: the weather window you have, and how long you really expect a coat to last. If you are sealing on a warm July weekend and plan to reseal in three years whatever the label says, Airport Grade does the job. If your only free weekend is in October, or you want the most durable film Latex-ite makes, Ultra Shield is the one. Our [Latex-ite driveway sealer reviews](/latex-ite-driveway-sealer-review/) cover how Airport Grade behaves on a typical faded driveway.

sections.h: What Do Ultra Shield and Airport Grade Have in Common?

blocks.p: More than most shoppers expect. The two data sheets match on almost everything that decides how the job goes:

ul: Chemistry: both are asphalt emulsions (fine droplets of asphalt in water) with polymer additives. Neither is a coal tar sealer, both list VOC content under 25 g/L, and both clean up with soap and water while wet. See [coal tar vs asphalt emulsion sealer](/coal-tar-vs-asphalt-emulsion-sealer/) for the other chemistries.
Pail: both come in 4.75-gallon pails weighing roughly 54 to 58 lbs depending on the sheet revision. Both are thick brown liquids that dry black.
Coverage: 400 to 500 square feet per pail on smooth or previously sealed driveways, 300 to 400 on rough or unsealed surfaces, and less on rough road-grade asphalt with large stone.
Coats: both call for thin coats, warn that thick coats cause uneven coverage, tracking and curing problems, and allow a second coat 24 hours after the first.
Cure: 24 to 48 hours at 70°F and 50% relative humidity, longer when it is cooler or more humid.
Rain: apply only when rain is not likely for 36 hours.
Applicator: a squeegee. Both sheets say a roller is the wrong tool and voids the warranty.

Prep: clean with a cleaner/degreaser, scrub oil and gas spots, prime oil stains with oil spot primer (half an hour to dry), let the surface dry completely (24 hours recommended), and wait at least one full season before sealing new asphalt.

sections.h: Which One Works in Colder Weather?

blocks.p: Ultra Shield, if your pail carries the 40°F rating. This is the biggest practical difference between the two. Airport Grade's data sheet calls for ground and air temperature of 55°F and rising and says to avoid applying when temperatures drop below 55°F. Ultra Shield's 2019 data sheet lists application at 40°F and rising, credited to ThermaSEAL, which it says cures in temperatures down to 40°F.

There is a catch worth flagging. An earlier Ultra Shield data sheet listed 55°F and rising, the same as Airport Grade, so not every pail on every shelf may carry the 40°F claim. Check the label before you plan a cool-weather job around it.

Even with ThermaSEAL, Latex-ite's own directions caution against applying late in the day, and say that early-spring or late-fall application, when the sun sits at a low angle, can prevent proper curing and cause tracking. A 40°F rating extends your season; it does not make a cold, cloudy, damp afternoon a good time to seal. Our guide to [what temperature to seal a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/) covers surface temperature and overnight lows.

sections.h: How Do the Film, Formula and UV Protection Differ?

blocks.p: Airport Grade is described as polymer fortified for strength and flexibility. Ultra Shield is described as using an Ultra Flex polymer system (a newer revision also mentions Nano-Guard technology) designed to adhere better to the driveway and to itself. A more flexible film is better at riding out the expansion and contraction of asphalt between hot days and cold nights. There is no independent lab data we could find comparing the two films, so treat this as Latex-ite's positioning rather than a measured difference.

Ultra Shield is sold as an EZ-Gel or Premium Gel formula, which Latex-ite says saves time and effort when spreading. Airport Grade is an EZ Stir formula. A gel holds on the squeegee and spreads more evenly with less effort, which helps a first-time DIYer keep the coat thin and even.

Ultra Shield lists UV protection with the claim that it stays black and will not fade or dull. Airport Grade's sheet makes no UV claim. All asphalt emulsions gray out over time in strong sun; a UV-resistant formula should slow that, which matters most on a south-facing, unshaded driveway.

Airport Grade's sheet says it fills hairline cracks, and Ultra Shield is also sold as a driveway filler sealer. Neither replaces a crack filler on anything wider than a hairline. Latex-ite's sheets say to let crack fillers cure 24 hours, or until firm, before sealing over them; see [how long driveway crack filler takes to dry](/how-long-does-driveway-crack-filler-take-to-dry/).

sections.h: What Do the 10-Year and 4- or 5-Year Ratings Mean?

blocks.p: Neither number predicts when you will need to reseal. Ultra Shield's sheets list a 10-year warranty. The Airport Grade sheet we found, revised in 2016, lists a 4-year warranty. The current product is sold as Airport Grade+ and is listed as a 5-year product, but we could not confirm that figure on a current Latex-ite data sheet, so read the pail.

A year rating on a sealer pail is a limited warranty or durability claim made under ideal conditions: thorough cleaning and oil-spot priming, a sound, crack-filled surface, thin squeegee coats, warm dry weather and no rain for 36 hours. Warranties typically cover the product, not the labor of reapplying it, and depend on following the directions; Latex-ite's own sheets say a roller voids the warranty.

Real-world life depends on traffic, sun, climate and film thickness. Thin asphalt-emulsion films wear first in tire paths and turning areas, and most homeowners reseal mid-tier consumer products every two to four years regardless of the rating. The better trigger is the surface itself: reseal when it turns gray and the stone starts to show. See [how long driveway sealer lasts](/how-long-does-driveway-sealer-last/) and [how often to seal a driveway](/how-often-to-seal-a-driveway/).

So read the ratings as a ranking within the brand. Latex-ite is telling you Ultra Shield is the more durable formula. Whether it is twice as durable is not something the labels prove, and if you reseal every three years anyway, the cold-weather window and the gel matter more than the extra warranty years.

blocks.p: Steep driveways deserve a note. Neither Latex-ite sheet we read gives a slope limit, but any sealer is harder to keep thin on a steep grade, and puddled areas at the bottom cure slowly and track. A gel formula is easier to control on a slope. Work across the slope and keep coats thin.

Comparing with Black Jack? Latex-ite's Ultra Shield lines up against Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 and Airport Grade against the Drive-Maxx 500 and 700. The biggest difference is that Drive-Maxx requires two coats every time. Our [Black Jack vs Latex-ite driveway sealer](/black-jack-vs-latex-ite-driveway-sealer/) comparison and the [Black Jack Drive-Maxx review](/black-jack-drive-maxx-review/) cover that side.

sections.h: How Many Pails of Ultra Shield or Airport Grade Do You Need?

blocks.p: The same number for either one, because the coverage figures are identical. Divide the driveway area by the per-pail figure for your surface and multiply by the number of coats. A 600 square foot driveway that was sealed a few years ago needs about 1,200 square feet of spreading for two coats, which is three pails at 400 to 500 square feet each. The same driveway, rough and never sealed, needs three to four pails at 300 to 400 square feet each.

Old, oxidized asphalt often drinks more than any label suggests, which is why our [Latex-ite review](/latex-ite-driveway-sealer-review/) plans on a more conservative 250 to 350 square feet a pail. Buy one spare pail you can return unopened, and buy every pail from one batch so the color matches. For the cost side, see [how much it costs to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/).

sections.h: How Do You Apply Either One Properly?

blocks.p: The two products share the same directions, so the steps are the same. Getting them right matters more than which pail you buy.

ol: Check the forecast: 55°F and rising for Airport Grade (40°F for Ultra Shield where the pail says so), no rain likely for 36 hours, and start early in the day.
Flip the pails at least 24 hours before, with the lids secure, so settled solids redistribute.
Clean and degrease: sweep, scrub oil and gas spots with cleaner/degreaser, rinse, and prime remaining oil stains with oil spot primer; let it dry half an hour.
Fill cracks wider than a hairline and let the filler cure (Latex-ite says 24 hours, or until firm).
Let the driveway dry completely; 24 hours is recommended. Mist lightly only if the pavement is very hot, and leave no puddles.
Box the pails: pour them back and forth between buckets so color and consistency match, and keep mixed pails covered.
Edge first with a large brush, protecting concrete with a tarp.

Pour a ribbon of sealer about 2 feet from the garage and pull it with the squeegee in a moon-shaped back-and-forth motion toward the street. Keep a wet edge, press for a thin coat and do not push the squeegee.
Finish in one session so no section cures at a different rate and dries a different shade.
Apply the second coat, if wanted, 24 hours later, then keep cars off for the 24-48 hour cure, longer in cool or humid weather.

blocks.p: Not sure about one coat or two? See [how many coats of driveway sealer](/how-many-coats-of-driveway-sealer/). If rain arrives early, see [rain after sealing a driveway](/rain-after-sealing-driveway/).

mistakes: Assuming every Ultra Shield pail allows 40°F

Only the 2019 Ultra Shield data sheet lists 40°F and rising; an earlier sheet listed 55°F. If your pail does not print the lower figure, plan the job as you would for Airport Grade: 55°F and rising, with a dry 36 hours ahead.
Paying for ten years on a driveway you will reseal in three

The warranty is a ranking inside Latex-ite's line, not a resealing schedule. If you reseal on a two- to three-year cycle anyway, or the asphalt will be overlaid soon, Airport Grade gives the same coverage and cure for less.
Both data sheets say to use a squeegee and state that a roller voids the warranty. A roller also lays a thinner, uneven film that wears through in the tire paths first.
Sealing late on a cool, low-sun day
Latex-ite warns that late-day, early-spring and late-fall application can stop the coat curing and cause tracking, even with ThermaSEAL. Start early on a sunny day so the film has warm hours to set.
bottomLine: Ultra Shield is the better product and Airport Grade is the better value. They cover the same 300 to 500 square feet per pail, cure in the same 24 to 48 hours and follow the same directions, so the choice comes down to weather and how long you expect a coat to last. Pay for Ultra Shield when you need its 40°F window (check the pail), want the UV claim on a sunny driveway or want the longest warranty. Otherwise buy Airport Grade, apply it thin with a squeegee on a warm, dry day, and reseal when the surface grays.

faqs.q: Is Latex-ite Ultra Shield better than Airport Grade?
faqs.a: Ultra Shield is Latex-ite's top-of-the-line sealer, with a 10-year warranty on its data sheet, a more flexible polymer system, a gel formula, a UV-protection claim and, on its 2019 sheet, a 40°F minimum against 55°F for Airport Grade. Coverage, cure time and rain window are the same. It is the better product; whether it is worth the extra money depends on your weather window and how often you reseal.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Latex-ite 10-year and 5-year sealers?
faqs.a: The year figure is the maker's warranty or durability rating under ideal conditions. Ultra Shield carries the 10-year rating. Airport Grade's 2016 sheet lists 4 years, and the current Airport Grade+ is sold as a 5-year product, so check the pail. Neither number predicts when you will reseal; most driveways need it every two to four years.

faqs.q: Is Ultra Shield a good asphalt sealer?
faqs.a: Yes, on a sound, properly prepared driveway. It is Latex-ite's premium polymer-modified asphalt emulsion with a gel formula and UV-protection claim. The same rules apply as for any emulsion: clean, dry, crack-filled asphalt, thin squeegee coats and 36 hours without rain. A premium pail laid over dust peels as fast as a cheap one.

faqs.q: Can I use Airport Grade as a second coat over Ultra Shield?
faqs.a: They are the same type of product from the same maker, so they are compatible. For a single job it is still better to use one product for both coats so the finish and cure are uniform and the warranty conditions are clearly met. For a future reseal, either can go over the other once the old coat is clean and sound.

faqs.q: How much area does one pail of Ultra Shield or Airport Grade cover?
faqs.a: Both data sheets give 400 to 500 square feet per 4.75-gallon pail on smooth or previously sealed driveways and 300 to 400 on rough or unsealed surfaces. Divide your driveway area by the figure for your surface and multiply by the number of coats. Very porous, oxidized asphalt can take more.

faqs.q: How long does Ultra Shield or Airport Grade take to dry?
faqs.a: Both data sheets list a cure of 24 to 48 hours at 70°F and 50% relative humidity, with a second coat allowed after 24 hours. Cooler or more humid weather lengthens it. Keep cars off for the full cure; see our guide to how long driveway sealer takes to dry for the stages.

faqs.q: Does Airport Grade hold up in hot, cold and snowy climates?
faqs.a: It is built for residential asphalt in normal US climates, but it needs 55°F and rising to apply and has no UV-protection claim. In harsh sun or freeze-thaw climates, Ultra Shield's more flexible polymers and UV claim make it the better fit. In any climate, timing the application well matters more than the product.
